title: 20VC — Coinbase Cuts AI Spend by 50% | Kalshi's $40B Valuation & Impending IPO | The Year for SaaS Roll-Ups
text: Coinbase's AI Cost Cuts, Anthropic vs. China, and the Microsoft Moat Question — Research Memo Thesis Enterprise AI spend is entering a "prove the ROI" phase — evidenced by open-source substitution compressing frontier-model economics (Coinbase) and boards gating further token spend on demonstrated lift (Lemkin's portfolio anecdote) — while frontier labs simultaneously pursue regulatory protection (Anthropic's Chinese-model complaint) to insulate themselves from that same price competition. Key Points Coinbase cut AI spend 50% QoQ while raising usage by shifting toward open-source models; O'Driscoll calls this a template every Fortune 500 CFO will replicate, and argues it will pressure frontier-model revenue growth, specifically naming Anthropic given open-source alternatives at "one-fifth the price." Lemkin doesn't dispute the data but is skeptical of the PR framing given Coinbase's own stock is down 30% last quarter. Lemkin raises (as an open question, not a settled view) whether open-source is impacting frontier-model growth "more than we predicted" — O'Driscoll is the one who makes the affirmative claim; this is not a shared conclusion between the two. Lemkin's live board-seat anecdote: a portfolio company hit its full H1 plan but was denied a token-spend doubling for the first time because it couldn't tie spend to ROI — direct evidence of governance-level scrutiny arriving even at healthy companies, independent of the open-source substitution dynamic. Anthropic petitioned the Senate Banking Committee alleging Chinese open-source labs are breaching ToS via mass-prompt distillation, seeking to restrict U.S. company use of Chinese models. O'Driscoll treats a ban as plausible partly because "in an era where SBF may get pardoned, this is pretty imaginable" (i.e., eroded institutional/regulatory norms), though he personally opposes an outright ban ("No... they should pay the naughty tax"). Lemkin calls the security framing "regulatory capture in the extreme," since the models run openly on U.S. inference. O'Driscoll's bubble-protection thesis: with ~40% of the S&P 500 tied to the AI trade, policy will protect incumbent AI valuations even if the outcome (e.g., banning cheap Chinese models) is bad policy — he explicitly likens it to 1982-era protectionism of IBM against PC clones ("so freaking dumb"). Microsoft's worst month since 2000 is attributed to lacking a standalone AI model — its story reduces to "capex funding OpenAI" while Cursor and Claude Code erode its developer-tool franchise from the application layer. Both treat Azure deceleration as a serious signal ("canary in the coal mine"), not noise. Market-breadth counter-signal: Bending Spoons IPO'ing at $20B is cited as proof the IPO window isn't frozen despite SpaceX IPO news; Lemkin forecasts a multi-year wave of "Bending Spoons-style" B2B roll-up IPOs. Kambi (sports-betting platform) is raising at $40B, up from $22B in May — flagged as an open question about whether sports betting or adjacent financial-product betting is the larger driver; no resolution given in the transcript. Consensus (not contrarian) items: both are skeptical of Chamath's 8090 as a part-time-founder vehicle, and both agree a founder at $1.5M ARR (growing to $5M) was rightly told this isn't Series A-ready, but should run a broad process ("meet 150 VCs") rather than take one rejection as final. Best Quotes "I have a portfolio company where every number is green... they wanted to double their token spend. For the first time, the board was like, 'Tie it to ROI.' And this amazing team couldn't." — Jason Lemkin. First-hand board-level evidence of AI-spend ROI scrutiny hitting even healthy companies. "If you have a cost structure that needs all that revenue, the last thing you need are cheap open-source alternatives at one-fifth the price. It's going to have some impact on the growth rate of companies like Anthropic." — Rory O'Driscoll. Specific, named bear thesis on frontier-model growth. "They don't have a standalone model... Cursor and Claude Code are eating the core parts of the Microsoft franchise." — Rory O'Driscoll. Structural (not cyclical) bear case on Microsoft's AI moat. "As an economy, we are so addicted to this—40% of the S&P 500 is tied to this bubble—that we're going to do everything we can to protect it." — Rory O'Driscoll. Frames AI-index concentration as a policy-protected systemic risk. Disagreements & Conviction Coinbase signal vs. noise: O'Driscoll holds a strong, analytically specific conviction this is a real leading indicator for frontier-model revenue risk; Lemkin's skepticism is about CEO optics/behavior, not the underlying economics — he explicitly doesn't dispute the data. AI ROI bull case vs. lived experience: Lemkin's board anecdote is a firsthand, high-conviction disconfirmation of the "AI capex always pays off" narrative — notably undercutting O'Driscoll's own framework that software companies should show revenue lift. Anthropic vs. China distillation: Lemkin holds the stronger, more absolute position ("zero risk," pure regulatory capture); O'Driscoll takes a moderate middle stance (enforce IP claims via penalty, not ban) but treats an eventual ban as plausible given institutional norm erosion (SBF-pardon comparison). Note: only O'Driscoll explicitly answers "no" to a ban; Lemkin's "I agree, don't touch my 401k" responds to the bubble-protection point, not the ban question directly — his stance on the ban itself is not explicitly stated. Microsoft — structural vs. mechanical framing: O'Driscoll's bear case is competitive-moat-based (named competitors: Cursor, Claude Code); Lemkin's is more about guidance/execution discipline ("any deceleration in Azure is a failure"). Not a true disagreement — different altitudes on the same call. title: No Priors — How Nuclear Will Unlock Energy Abundance with Valar Atomics Founder Isaiah Taylor
text: Valor Atomics: Hardware-Execution Nuclear Bet — Research Memo Thesis Valor Atomics claims to have broken the "paper reactor" pattern that has stalled US nuclear for 50 years by treating reactors as iterated manufactured hardware rather than modeling/simulation projects — evidenced by an actual criticality (November) and first power generation days before this taping. The investment case rests entirely on whether this single 100kW DOE-authority demonstration can convert into repeatable NRC-licensed commercial scale, which the transcript does not resolve. Key Points Valor's reactor (100kW, ~10^17 fissions/sec) went critical in November and made power for the first time days before recording, operating under DOE testing authority via an executive order for advanced reactor demonstrations — not the NRC's commercial licensing pathway. Core segmentation framework for the SMR sector: "hardware execution" companies (Valor) vs. "design/modeling" companies ("paper reactors"). Taylor claims most nuclear startups are the latter. Verticalization is the stated cost/speed moat: in-house Reactor Protection System built in 6 weeks for $400K vs. a $5M/2-year vendor quote; custom rebar-free concrete formulation (rebar becomes neutron-activated) enabling a 78-inch bio-shield stacked in 42 hours without grout/bolts/screws. Safety architecture is consequence-based, not probability-based: design assumes total systems failure and relies on passive physics (RCCS boil/condense natural circulation, no moving parts) to prevent any public radiation dose. A live scram-and-full-power-cutoff demonstration was planned for days after this recording — outcome not in transcript. Financing structure: equity-only (no project-finance/debt participation yet). Taylor frames this as investors underwriting "technical execution risk," explicitly conceding debt markets haven't yet validated the model. Go-to-market is power-first, not contract-first: build gigawatt capacity with land/fiber and let data-center demand follow, rather than securing PPAs before building. Market-sizing claim: energy is price-elastic ("if you reduce price, you increase demand"), so Taylor frames Valor's TAM as "fundamentally infinite" and independent of AI-specific demand — despite the AI/Nvidia demo being the visible current wedge. Named consensus benchmark (per host, not guest): big compute buyers reportedly believe no new nuclear capacity can deliver at scale until 2031–2032. Taylor's response reframes why buyers believe this (nuclear-startup history is simulation-heavy) rather than disputing the date directly. Best Quotes "Energy being a commodity, the demand is set by the price. If you can figure out how to make energy cheaper, you will have demand." — Isaiah Taylor. States the price-elasticity thesis underpinning the "infinite market" claim. "We had to invent our own grade of concrete... We even built our own Reactor Protection System (RPS) in six weeks for $400,000 when we were quoted $5 million and two years." — Isaiah Taylor. Concrete, quantified evidence of the verticalization strategy's cost/time compression on one safety subsystem. "We know the physics works and there is infinite demand. We are asking investors to underwrite technical execution risk, which is what Silicon Valley is best at." — Isaiah Taylor. Explicit statement that this is equity-financed conviction, not yet debt/project-finance-validated. "If I have a gigawatt of power with land and fiber, someone will put a data center there... The load will follow." — Isaiah Taylor. Reveals a power-first (not PPA-first) development strategy with real merchant/counterparty risk. Disagreements & Conviction Guest vs. compute-buyer consensus on timeline : Buyers reportedly see 2031–2032 as the earliest scaled delivery; Taylor doesn't dispute the date but argues it's derived from comparing Valor to simulation-heavy peers — a structural, calibrated counter-argument rather than a bold re-forecast. Conviction: high but diagnostic, not a numeric claim. "Infinite demand" framing vs. AI-driven founding wedge : Taylor downplays AI as the causal driver even while showcasing an Nvidia Blackwell demo — a real rhetorical tension, likely deliberate positioning to avoid being pigeonholed as an AI-datacenter vendor. Watch for actual customer concentration. Equity conviction vs. absent debt market validation : Taylor asserts the physics is "solved," yet by his own account no project-finance/debt capital has followed — the more disinterested market signal contradicts the confidence level of his own language. Nuclear safety-statistics framing is not actually contrarian : Deaths-per-TWh data favoring nuclear (including rooftop-solar fall fatalities) is well-established among energy analysts; Taylor presents it as a hidden truth, which mildly overstates his own novelty (public-perception gap ≠ analytical contrarianism). Unresolved structural gap : The entire "planetary scale" thesis depends on the NRC's slow, precedent-bound commercial licensing regime — the transcript gives no detail on how one DOE-authority demonstration reactor becomes a pathway to serial NRC-licensed production. This is the largest unaddressed risk, not explicitly acknowledged by the guest. Investment Implications Financing structure (12–36mo financing; 3–7yr proof) : VC/growth equity, not utilities or project-finance debt, captures early SMR economics — inverts the traditional power-generation capital stack. Affected: Oklo, NuScale, Kairos Power, X-energy, utility IPPs (Vistra, Talen, Constellation), infra debt funds. [Transcript-supported financing fact; replication/crowded-trade dynamic is inference.] Power-first development model (5–10yr, contingent on gigawatt-scale build) : If viable, shifts leverage from hyperscalers (who currently dictate PPA terms) toward power+land+fiber developers, potentially compressing the "AI power scarcity premium" priced into nuclear/gas-peaker equities. Affected: Constellation, Vistra, Talen, data-center REITs

title: Hidden Forces — Schrödinger's Strait and the New Energy Order | Daniel Yergin
text: Daniel Yergin on Hormuz, China's Resilience, and the End of Easy Globalization — Research Memo Thesis The Iran/Hormuz and Ukraine crises both failed to produce the feared oil-price catastrophe because supply chains, inventories, and US swing-producer status absorbed the shock faster than models predicted — but Yergin's own caveats (historically low inventories, unresolved Iranian intent to institutionalize control of Hormuz, Iran's unresolved rational-vs-ideological duality) argue the system is deferred-fragile, not durably resilient. Key Points Neither Ukraine nor the Hormuz crisis produced the modeled price catastrophe: Saudi bypass pipelines (built after the Iran-Iraq tanker war), the US's shift to largest oil/gas exporter, IEA-coordinated strategic-stock releases, and Asian demand rationing all absorbed the shock. The single biggest surprise per Yergin was China: it drew down outsized strategic reserves and cut imports rather than bidding up price, which is why the market never saw $200/bbl oil. Per Trump's own account (as relayed by Yergin), the US pushed the MOU because inventories were headed toward "the bottom of the tank" by end-July, risking "bedlam"/depression-level disruption. Yergin: the dire scenario was averted, but inventories "still are very low in historic terms" — the system has less buffer for the next shock, not more. The June MOU is deliberately ambiguous; Iran has set up a Persian Gulf Strait Authority and Persian Gulf Insurance Company, signaling intent to functionally toll/control Hormuz as an "Iranian canal" — a durable institutional claim, not a temporary posture, even as Trump denies Iran will control it. On China/Malacca: Yergin did not endorse the idea that US strategic planners should rethink choke-point leverage over China (that framing was the host's, not confirmed by the guest). What Yergin actually established is narrower: China's South China Sea militarization and massive storage buildup show China itself fears a Malacca-style blockade (WWII "scarecrows" analogy), i.e., defensive hedging, not proof that US leverage is diminished. China is a structural beneficiary: EVs were 1-in-4 global car sales last year (mostly Chinese-made) vs. ~7% in the US; China also produces ~90% of world solar panels and dominates batteries. The crisis functions as inadvertent marketing for Chinese EV/renewables exports into the Global South. China's energy strategy diversifies import sources across the Middle East/Iran (cheap Iranian oil, more from Arab states) while simultaneously deepening reliance on discounted Russian barrels — Yergin explicitly calls Russia "an economic vassal of China" that exports oil and gas to it. This sits in tension with China's stated "lesson of Europe" (avoid over-dependence on one supplier). OPEC fragmentation: UAE exited OPEC mid-crisis (third defector in seven years); Iraq is threatening exit over quotas. Saudi Arabia "has made clear it's not going to curtail its production so that other people can increase." Combined with Iran's return to exporting at capacity, Yergin flags a plausible swing back to the pre-crisis low-$60s oversupply regime — though he still frames OPEC as "not going away," a hedged, non-contrarian call. Iran is held by Yergin as genuinely bimodal: an "expert negotiator" and economic actor (Strait Authority, Insurance Company, "money-making deal") but also "first and foremost an ideological movement" (cites regime's killing of 40,000 protesters earlier this year as evidence of resilience/ideological commitment). Yergin does not resolve which dominates — treats the duality itself as the central uncertainty. Grid/electricity: AI and data-center demand is driving a genuine step-change in load growth (a Southeast US utility CEO cited demand growth moving from ~0.5%/year to 8% in one year — "when your demand is growing like that, you have to hustle"). Yergin frames grid reliability as a subset of energy security, with permitting as the binding constraint, not capital. Gulf states are hedging away from sole reliance on the US: developing independent security capacity and their own inventories/pipelines, diversifying alignments (Iran-Oman talks; UAE-Israel-US vs. Turkey-Saudi axes); their sovereign wealth funds (multi-trillion dollar) are major independent global capital allocators, increasingly decoupled from the oil price cycle. Yergin flags Europe's deindustrialization/competitiveness loss, compounded by the Gulf crisis "accentuating the crisis in NATO," as an underdiscussed structural risk — offered without quantitative support. Best Quotes "We never saw the kind of $200 barrel oil that people thought would happen" — Yergin, on why Chinese inventory drawdowns (not just pipelines/US supply) were the real shock absorber; the central mechanism thesis of the episode. "They've set up the Persian Gulf Strait Authority and the Persian Gulf Insurance Company... they see their control as both political leverage... and a money-making deal" — Yergin, evidence Iran intends durable institutional control of Hormuz, not a ceasefire posture. "Russia has basically become an economic vassal of China. So it exports oil and natural gas to China." — Yergin, a striking, non-consensus characterization of Russia-China energy dependency with direct relevance to Russian crude discount durability and sanctions-evasion capacity. "When your demand is growing like that, you have to hustle." — Yergin, relaying a Southeast US utility CEO's demand growth jumping from ~0.5% to 8% — the concrete data point behind the AI/data-center grid-investment thesis. Disagreements & Conviction Resilience narrative vs. Yergin's caveats (moderate-firm): Host frames the story as "nightmare that didn't happen"; Yergin agrees on the surface but repeatedly qualifies — "we're not going to go back to what things were before," inventories "still are very low." title: Odd Lots — How a Major Grocery Store Chain Can Dramatically Lower the Cost of Food | Odd Lots
text: Aldi's Anti-CPG Grocery Model: SKU Rationalization, No Slotting Fees, and the Urban Discount Bet — Research Memo Thesis Aldi's cost advantage over conventional grocers is structural, not scale-driven: radical SKU reduction (2,000 vs. tens of thousands) and near-total private-label control eliminate slotting fees and compress labor/restocking costs, enabling Aldi to open a profitable discount format in one of the most expensive retail corridors in the US (adjacent to Times Square). This is a durable operating-model moat, not a temporary price gap, with read-throughs for legacy grocers' shelf-fee economics and mid-tier branded CPG. Key Points Core structural advantage: ~2,000 SKUs (4,000 varieties) vs. 30–40 ketchup SKUs or 60 olive oil SKUs at typical grocers; Patton: "there are no slotting fees" at Aldi, which he attributes directly to why competitors carry deep, supplier-subsidized assortments. Private-label control (not brand-name carry) is the enabler of nearly every other efficiency: custom multi-barcode packaging (cashier never twists the item), display-ready cases, and fast supply response to viral trends (sourdough now >500,000 loaves/week; feta sales spiked with viral recipe trend). Concrete labor/opex data points: restocking olive oil takes ~2% of the time versus a conventional store; digital shelf labels saved 3–4 hours/store/week of manual sign-changing (Patton is explicit this is NOT used for dynamic/surge pricing). Scale context: over 2,600 Aldi locations underpins 3–4 year advance grower contracting (can't rely on local spot markets). New ~25,000 sq ft Times Square-adjacent store (Aldi's 2nd Manhattan location, 14th in NY area) is a genuine bet that the low-SKU/low-labor model can be profitable at premium urban rents — Patton: intended to be very profitable, not just a "billboard." Self-checkout was skipped there specifically for real-estate-allocation/existing-efficiency reasons — a separate rationale from the general industry constraint (RFID still uneconomical for produce/age-verification items), which applies only ~1/3 of stores fleet-wide. Macro trade-down signal: beef prices at 70-year highs are pushing customers to ground turkey/chicken (30–40% cheaper); simultaneously, GLP-1-linked protein demand is accelerating across adjacent categories (protein bagels, popcorn, sparkling water) alongside a fiber/bean resurgence. Brand-architecture shift underway: per the host, Aldi is consolidating from ~90 private-label brands to ~23; Patton confirms the driver was customer confusion and a prior failure to put the Aldi logo on-pack (the specific 90→23 figures are the host's framing, not independently confirmed by Patton in his own words). Best Quotes "It's about shelf space and suppliers paying to be on the shelf. At Aldi, there are no slotting fees." — Guest. Names the specific mechanism that inflates conventional grocery/CPG cost structures — the clearest non-consensus structural claim in the transcript. "We have 2,000 SKUs in the store, covering 4,000 varieties. I'd ask the customer: do you really need 40 choices of ketchup?" — Guest. Quantifies the SKU-rationalization thesis underlying Aldi's price gap. "We don't do dynamic pricing; we would never do that." — Guest. Categorical, unhedged denial despite having the enabling technology (digital labels) — a deliberate trust/brand-positioning stance amid live industry controversy over surge pricing. "Restocking our olive oil takes 2% of the time it takes at another store." — Guest. A concrete, extreme labor-productivity benchmark for comps work. Disagreements & Conviction Genuine host-guest friction is thin in this transcript; the one unambiguous tension is dynamic pricing: Joe's question implicitly raises the market's surge-pricing suspicion of digital shelf labels, and Patton flatly forecloses it ("we would never do that") — high conviction, categorically stated. SKU-reduction-as-consumer-benefit (Patton's framing) vs. industry-standard deep-assortment practice is non-consensus relative to how most grocers operate/monetize shelf space, but it is Aldi's known strategy rather than a contested claim — stated with strong, unhedged conviction ("do you really need 40 choices of ketchup?"). "Aisle of Shame" origin (European lack of big-box competitors) vs. current deliberate merchandising/engagement tool (4M-member fan group) is a minor legacy-quirk-vs-strategy tension, not a real contradiction — moderate conviction, anecdotal, no basket-lift figures given. Investment Implications First-order: Slotting-fee elimination and SKU rationalization structurally squeeze mid-tier branded CPG (weak-differentiation condiments/oils) and pressure the hidden slotting-fee profit center that subsidizes thin margins at legacy grocers (Kroger, Albertsons). Time horizon: multi-year, structural. [Confidence: mechanism is transcript-supported; competitive margin-erosion conclusion is inference.] First-order: Beef-price-driven trade-down to chicken/turkey benefits poultry processors and discount-format volume; protein/fiber demand acceleration favors CPG players that can reformulate quickly. Time horizon: near-term, already playing out. [Confidence: trade-down fact is transcript-supported; any cattle-cycle-ceiling read is inference and not supported by this transcript.] Second-order (inference): Aldi's private-label supply agility (reallocating "line time" within months) may let it capture viral food-trend demand disproportionately versus brand-dependent retailers — a channel-concentration effect, not a rising-tide-for-all-CPG story. [Confidence: low-medium; speculative extrapolation from two data points (feta, sourdough).] Second-order (inference): The Times Square store tests whether Aldi's low-labor model can outcompete incumbent NYC chains (Morton Williams, Gristedes) on rent economics in premium urban corridors — relevant to urban grocery-anchored retail real estate and incumbent margin risk. title: Excess Returns — Labor Market Cracks, Wild Fed Credibility Data and Semis Running Out of Pie | Last Call
text: Excess Returns "Last Call" — AI Capex, Fed Narrative, and Vol Fragility — Research Memo Thesis The month's dominant, cross-confirmed signal is that near-term market moves (SpaceX's listing, tech vol spasms, semicap re-ratings) are increasingly driven by mechanical positioning and narrative flows rather than fundamentals — while underneath, real economic data (job quality, refining margins) is quietly deteriorating in ways headline metrics obscure. Key Points SpaceX's IPO opened higher, spiked for two days, then sold off sharply but remained above its opening print (host's correction to the "fell like a rock" framing) — framed by Jack Forehand as a flows/front-running story tied to NASDAQ's July 7th index inclusion, not a fundamentals repricing. Andy Constan's macro thesis: aggregate real earnings growth is capped by real GDP, and too many AI-exposed stocks are pricing in earnings growth the "pie" can't support ("oversubscribed"). Current winners span the hardware stack — memory/storage, chipmakers (Nvidia, AMD, Intel), and equipment makers (Tokyo Electron, ASML, KLA, Applied Materials, Lam Research, the "Fab Five") — with the Fab Five's stocks specifically the "most parabolic," not the exclusive winners. Hyperscalers may be margin-compressed since they're subsidizing token pricing. Ben Hunt's narrative-analytics data: the "Fed losing credibility" narrative (peak roughly one year before this recording, per Hunt's relative timestamp — exact calendar date not stated) has collapsed while a "Fed gaining credibility" narrative is rising sharply; Hunt links this directly to gold via his framework ("price of gold = 1/trust"). Brent Kochuba's options-flow data: his "Core 1M" metric dropping below 8 preceded the early-June ~7% two-day NASDAQ drawdown and recurred around June 20th; he sees setup for "a pretty sharp correction or a resyncing of volatility." Supporting data point: >80% of QQQ volume trades in ≤5-day expirations. Eric Basmajian's labor data: recent job growth is concentrated in healthcare/social-assistance (elder care, tied to boomer retirement), paying ~$35K/year — his framing: "that's not resilience; that's sustenance," and the Fed's headline count lacks a wealth-weighted view of job quality. Basmajian's oil data: US crack spread at $62/barrel vs. a $15–20 historical norm; he argues gasoline prices will stay structurally elevated (crack spread $60–70) even if crude retraces to $80–90. Forward call: Jack Forehand (echoing Jeremy Grantham) argues the next AI phase isn't "everything goes up" — hyperscalers that operated as separate "islands" are now competing directly, compressing margins across the stack. Best Quotes "Future earnings growth is oversubscribed... there's just not enough pie for all of them to be successful." — Guest (Andy Constan). Core market-wide valuation-risk framework, not just an AI-specific bubble call. "No one cares about the fundamentals of SpaceX right now... everybody is front-running [NASDAQ's July 7th addition]." — Guest (Jack Forehand), citing Dave Nadig as corroboration. Frames a dated, mechanical catalyst as the dominant near-term price driver, decoupled from fundamentals. "Job growth is really all healthcare... those people make about $35,000 a year... that's not resilience; that's sustenance." — Guest (Eric Basmajian). Undercuts the "resilient labor market" narrative the Fed and equity bulls lean on. "The crack spread as of this morning was $62 per barrel. Normal is between $15 and $20... even if oil prices go back to $80 or $90, you will see gas prices at a crack spread of $60 or $70, which is higher than they've ever been." — Guest (Eric Basmajian). A refining-bottleneck inflation-transmission signal independent of crude direction. Disagreements & Conviction Jack Forehand vs. host's initial "shoeshine boy" retail-euphoria framing on SpaceX: Jack's flows/front-running view is delivered with high, unhedged conviction ("No one cares about the fundamentals... right now") and appears to be the settled read. Internal tension within Constan's own argument: AI could grow the total earnings pie (productivity gains, hedged: "it's possible") vs. his more forceful, specific claim that current AI-earnings expectations are already oversubscribed. Unresolved by Constan himself — his real call is a relative-value trade within AI (equipment/chip makers vs. hyperscalers), not a broad anti-AI bubble call. Basmajian vs. Fed/consensus reading of payrolls: high-conviction, falsifiable composition critique ("that's not resilience; that's sustenance") asserting a specific institutional blind spot (no wealth-weighted count). Basmajian vs. "oil price governs gas price" shorthand: high conviction, stated near-factually ("the crack spread does not lie"). Kochuba vs. bullish options positioning: moderate conviction, appropriately hedged ("I think we're setting up here for...") — a probabilistic structural/flow call, not a certainty. Note: Ben Hunt's Fed-credibility segment is descriptive narrative-tracking, not a contrarian stance — he isn't disputing anyone's view, just presenting the data shift. Investment Implications Semicap/chip complex (medium-term, 2–4 quarters): AI capex flows are currently rewarding the whole hardware stack, with equipment makers (Fab Five) showing the most parabolic moves. First-order: continued re-rating as capex flows through. Second-order (inference): this is a crowded, reflexive trade pricing hyperscaler capex budgets rather than end AI-revenue — a wobble in any hyperscaler's spending plan could cascade across ASML, Tokyo Electron, KLA, Applied Materials, Lam Research, Nvidia, AMD, Intel simultaneously. QQQ/mega-cap tech options structure (near-term, weeks): Short-dated (≤5 DTE) options dominate volume, per Kochuba, meaning vol spasms are increasingly mechanical/flow-driven. title: Yet Another Value — $VEON: a busted EM telecom hiding a 4x? | Samit Umatiya, UIG Funds
text: Veon (VEON) — Sum-of-the-Parts EM Telecom/Fintech Thesis — Research Memo Thesis Veon is a five-market EM telecom holding company whose 84.6% Kyivstar stake already covers more than half its market cap, leaving the market to effectively ignore four growing digital/fintech businesses (notably JazzCash in Pakistan). The thesis is real but rests on a valuation bridge the guest himself could not reconcile with the host's live counter-math — this is a promising, under-covered idea that needs independent balance-sheet and EV verification before sizing. Key Points Structure: Veon (formerly VimpelCom, founded 1991, first Russian NYSE listing 1995) has consolidated from 18 countries to six, divested Russia post-invasion, and now operates in Ukraine, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan. Kyivstar: 84.6% stake, guest values at ~$2.8B (stated once) / ~$2B (stated later, see inconsistency below) — either way, over half of Veon's market cap. Non-Ukraine assets: ~$3.24B of 2025 revenue growing mid-to-high teens; guest values these at ~$700M equity / ~$2.1B EV, calling a 1x revenue multiple "very conservative" and arguing this implies the four non-Ukraine markets are ~66% of total EV. JazzCash (Pakistan fintech): processes ~$60B in transaction value (~15% of Pakistan's GDP), never independently valued; management has acknowledged exploring a strategic sale, spin-off, or IPO; pursuing a full digital banking license (unlocks wealth management + remittances, ~30% of Pakistan's GDP). Pakistan digital financial services revenue grew $156M (2023) → $277M (2024) → $377M (2025) per the 20-F. Forward FCF target: management guides $900M–$1B equity free cash flow by 2027; guest applies a 15x multiple to imply ~$15B equity value (~4x current market cap). Net debt ex-leases ~1.0–1.1x EBITDA; $100M buyback initiated. "AI 1440" / Kaza LLM: Veon is building localized LLMs (Kaza LLM) tailored to linguistic/cultural context, servicing ~1 million rural customer journeys/month (healthcare, credit access via AI). Framed as a "sovereign AI moat" global tech giants can't easily replicate — no monetization metrics given. Bundling/retention: multi-play users (telecom + fintech + healthcare + ride-hailing/Uklon) show 66% higher retention than voice-only users — core argument for why Starlink is a partner, not a disruptor, post-war. EV bridge is unresolved and internally inconsistent. Host's balance-sheet calc (~75M shares × $50 + $4B non-current debt + $1B current debt − $1.7B cash) computes to ~$7.0–7.3B (host rounded to "~$8B" — his own rounding is loose). Guest's numbers shift between two passes of the same conversation: Kyivstar stake valued at "$2.8B" against a "$4.9B" EV early on, then "$2B" against a "$5.1B" EV later, yielding a "$3.1B" residual. The guest's own figures don't agree with each other, independent of the host/guest gap. This is the single load-bearing number for the entire non-Kyivstar SOTP case and it is not solid. Letter One overhang: ~45% of Veon owned by Letter One, sanctioned by EU/US/Ukraine. Guest: "reputational harm," banks/suppliers "might be reluctant to engage," and "I haven't heard anything from management regarding Letter One" — a stated information gap, not a resolved view. If you apply a 1x revenue multiple, which is very conservative, the four non-Ukraine markets alone are worth about 66% of Veon's total EV." — Guest. Core SOTP thesis in one breath. "The JazzCash fintech business in Pakistan is worth isolating... It has never been independently valued. Management has acknowledged they are looking to crystallize that value, whether through a strategic investor, spin-off, or IPO." — Guest. Concrete, management-sourced catalyst. "My napkin math was based on a $3.4 billion market cap and $1.7 billion in net debt, giving a $5.1 billion EV. If you subtract the $2 billion portion of Kyivstar, the residual EV is $3.1 billion." — Guest. Diverges from both the host's live counter-calc and the guest's own earlier figures — the numbers a PM must independently rebuild before underwriting. "It certainly creates reputational harm... I haven't heard anything from management regarding Letter One. I think it's a risk you just have to be comfortable holding through." — Guest. Candid admission of an unresolved information gap on the key overhang — note the host, not the guest, later floats "retire the stake at a discount" as upside; the guest never responds (interview ends immediately after). Disagreements & Conviction EV math (host vs. guest, and guest vs. himself) — unresolved, not a considered rebuttal. The guest restates inputs rather than reconciling with the host's figure, and his own Kyivstar valuation/EV shift between two points in the same conversation ($2.8B/$4.9B vs. $2B/$5.1B). Low conviction as stated; this is the thesis's weakest link. "No coverage" as evidence of mispricing — guest conviction is moderate but this is a fairly generic under-followed-microcap framing, not sharp edge; absence of coverage ≠ mispricing. "Telecom" vs. "tech" reframing vs. his own methodology — guest wants to drop the "telecom" label and calls Veon a tech company, yet values the non-Ukraine digital assets on a 1x revenue multiple, a legacy-telecom-style metric, not a fintech/GMV-adjusted approach. Rhetorically high conviction, methodologically inconsistent. Capital controls — guest downplays repatriation risk from martial-law-era Ukraine controls, citing HoldCo buyback capacity as proof; doesn't address whether Kyivstar-level cash specifically can move up to the parent. Moderate-high stated conviction, not fully substantiated. Letter One "upside optionality" — this idea belongs to the host , floated as an unanswered question in the final exchange; the guest never engages with or endorses it (interview ends). title: All-In — AI Sovereignty Wars, Palantir-Nvidia Deal, SCOTUS Birthright Ruling, Newsom’s CA Budget Lie
text: All-In Podcast Ep. 279 — AI Sovereignty, Frontier Lab Trust Crisis & California Fiscal Risk — Research Memo Thesis Enterprises are pulling back from frontier-model dependency (Anthropic/OpenAI) because they fear their proprietary data and IP will be used to vertically integrate against them (per the Figma/Claude Design precedent) — a trend that favors sovereign/on-prem AI infrastructure (Palantir-Nvidia) and orchestration/harness layers over pure API-token revenue. Separately, California's fiscal position is described by the panel as approaching a genuine solvency crisis, a distinct but non-consensus muni/state-credit risk raised in the same episode. Key Points Palantir + Nvidia announced a "Sovereign AI Operating System" (using Nvidia's Neotron open models, as named in transcript — likely "Nemotron," flagged as unconfirmed) letting US government agencies retain ownership of hardware, data, and model weights. Sacks: Anthropic allegedly blindsided partner Figma by launching a competing "Claude Design" vertical (per The Information ; Anthropic's CPO sat on Figma's board, resigning only 3 days before launch); Figma stock down ~50% YTD. Anthropic has since launched Science, Security, Legal, Financial, and Code verticals — a Microsoft/Google-style platform-then-vertical-capture playbook. Chamath (8090, self-interested test): wrapping Claude in their own harness was 1.4x cheaper/1.5x faster than Anthropic Opus alone; wrapping the best open-source model was 16.4x cheaper. His conclusion: enterprises not pursuing independent model access are "derelict and irresponsible." Also cites a BCG stat that half of large US companies fail to earn above their cost of capital, framing urgency for AI-driven productivity gains. Friedberg: life-sciences and other data-rich enterprises are broadly refusing Anthropic's "share data for early access" offers; forecasts industry shift from few large model "hubs" to large + medium hubs plus distributed enterprise-run inference "spokes." Export controls on Anthropic's model (named "Mythos"/"Fable 5" in transcript, ambiguous/possibly transcript naming quirks) were imposed via a letter, then rescinded ~2 weeks later, restoring customer access — no reinstatement occurred (correcting an exec-summary error). Sacks attributes the episode to three coincident factors (Dario publicly calling it a "cyber weapon," Amazon reporting failed guardrails, refusal to patch a jailbreak) — but the transcript is ambiguous on whether these three factors explain the imposition or the removal of controls. Sacks cautions against over-extrapolating this into a durable policy shift; default administration posture is "pro-innovation, pro-export, pro-infrastructure." Sacks: banning Chinese open-source model imports is self-defeating — once open-sourced, a model can be forked and run entirely on US hardware with no data flowing back to China. Friedberg: the AI-jobs-apocalypse narrative from ~2 years ago "is not reality" — AI adoption is "clunky," not a discontinuous shock; forecasts AI creates more jobs than it destroys (unhedged, single-speaker claim, no pushback from panel). California: Friedberg calls Newsom's $351B "balanced" budget (through 2028) an accounting trick — budget grew from $215B (2019) to $355B today, alongside $1.4T in public debt and pension liabilities senior to state bonds; predicts a default serious enough to test federal-bailout politics. Chamath forecasts a "wholesale replacement" of the California Constitution via redistricting and a "complete red wave." Scope note: the transcript also covers ~15 lines on the Supreme Court's birthright-citizenship ruling (Trump v. Barbara, 6-3) with distinct Sacks (14th Amendment original-intent), Chamath (assimilation/cultural cohesion), and Friedberg ("makers vs. takers") framings. Omitted here as non-investment-relevant; flagged per QA audit so its absence is a deliberate scoping choice, not an oversight. Best Quotes "The basic view among enterprises in this country is, 'I'm going to chill out and waste my time with tokens. I'm going to get no value and they're going to get my IP.'" — Alex Karp (clip) — the core enterprise-trust thesis driving demand for sovereign AI. "Anthropic blindsided its then-business partner with the launch of 'Claude Design.' ... Anthropic has also launched Claude Science, Security, Legal, Financial, and Code." — Sacks — named, concrete evidence of the vertical-integration risk to anyone building atop frontier-lab APIs. "When you use our harness with Claude, it was 1.4x cheaper and 1.5x faster than Anthropic Opus alone. But if you wrap the open-source model with our software factory, it was 16.4x cheaper." — Chamath — quantified (if self-interested) evidence that value is migrating to the orchestration layer. "$1.4 trillion in public debt and massive unfunded pension liabilities that sit senior to state bonds... this state is on the brink of a default so significant that if the federal government is called in to bail them out, the rest of the union will ask why they should pay for it." — Friedberg — the most quantified, actionable claim in the episode on CA muni/credit risk. Disagreements & Conviction Karp's CNBC appearance — theater or substance? Host frames it as a "televised nervous breakdown"; Sacks flatly rejects this ("nothing of the sort... first clue that he's actually saying something insightful"). High conviction from Sacks; sets up the sovereignty thesis as strategic doctrine rather than personality noise. Frontier-lab distrust is panel consensus, not internal disagreement. All four speakers agree enterprises shouldn't trust proprietary data to Anthropic/OpenAI. This is positioned as contrarian to the Silicon Valley/sell-side narrative, but there is no genuine tension among the four speakers themselves — worth noting since it's framed as "non-consensus" only relative to the broader market. title: The Compound — Brian Belski Returns! | TCAF 249
text: Brian Belski (Humalis) — Second-Half Outlook — Research Memo Thesis Belski stays structurally bullish (25-year secular bull, 7-10 years left) but warns of a "second derivative less positive" second half — large-cap earnings growth decelerating from 20-25% toward a more normal 10-12% pace — while continuing to favor the broadening-out trade (small/mid-cap, regional bank consolidation) over mega-cap concentration. His own words also sketch the mechanism (hyperscaler capex reversal → multiple compression) that could end the cycle, though he doesn't think it's imminent. Key Points 2H setup: Expects choppier, less linear markets as large-cap earnings growth normalizes from 20-25% to the 10-12% typical of an earnings-driven market. "I think there's too many bulls out there." Broadening-out trade reiterated: Small-cap forward (next-12-month) earnings growth ~28% vs. 23-24% for large-cap; financials — specifically regional bank consolidation (smaller banks in Montana, Wyoming, Idaho, the South taking share from majors) — cited as the driver. Hyperscaler capex skepticism: Believes AI-capex-fueled earnings growth "has to slow down," and is openly skeptical of management guidance to the contrary ("of course they are telling you that—they want to go to the marketplace"). Stock picks: Bullish Microsoft (34% ROE, 25% earnings growth vs. -23% YTD price — calls the gap unjustified), Oracle ("unjustly being punished"), Palantir, and beaten-down exchanges CME/CBOE/Nasdaq/ICE (sold off on new-competition fears; he calls them "cheap," not existentially threatened). Meta — bifurcated, unresolved view: Praises Meta as the best AI monetizer on earth (Reels/Instagram) but distrusts its capital allocation, citing the $80B metaverse spend/loss. No buy/avoid call given in transcript. Tail risk named explicitly: Floats a 2001-style tech-overcapacity analog — if AI capex reverses, it "hits multiples at the same time" as earnings, risking recession. Best hedge if worried about the AI trade: buy software (stated flatly, not hedged); a broader software-cycle "renaissance" is separately hedged with "I hope so." AI-bubble pushback: Per the host's recap of a prior Belski call, he has argued against the "AI bubble" framing on Mag 7 by pointing to increasingly uncorrelated earnings reactions within the group — Belski does not re-argue or elaborate on this himself in this conversation. Business update: Humalis is a model-provider (non-competing with advisor clients) — 3 North American ETFs + 1 mutual fund (Canada), 5 SMAs (US), AUM approaching $500M, aspirational target of "one trillion. I hope." Self-disclosed epistemic caveat: Belski himself frames his forecasting record as mixed, not uniformly accurate ("You got to get some things right. Get a lot of stuff wrong.") — worth weighting into how much conviction to assign his calls. Best Quotes "Beware of the 'second derivative less positive'... earnings are going to slow down a little bit for large-cap stocks." — Belski; core 2H thesis: still bullish trend, decelerating growth, more chop. "Small-cap earnings growth for the next 12 months is 28%; large-cap is 23% to 24%." — Belski; concrete, falsifiable number underpinning the rotation call. "It has to slow down. They say it's not, but of course they are telling you that—they want to go to the marketplace." — Belski; explicit distrust of hyperscaler capex guidance. "I think we're going to have a recession at some point... what happens when these capex trends go into reverse? That hits multiples at the same time." — Belski; names the exact mechanism for how the bull case could break, echoing 2001. Disagreements & Conviction Secular bull vs. recession admission (internal tension, not host pushback): High-conviction bull call ("still on board... 7 to 10 years left") sits alongside a tentative, musing-toned recession/2001-overcapacity risk. Read as: stay long the trend, but hyperscaler capex guidance is the tripwire to watch. AI-bubble pushback: Presented by the host as Belski's past call (dispersion in Mag 7 earnings reactions as evidence against a monolithic bubble). Belski does not restate or defend this in his own words here — treat conviction as inferred from his continued single-name mega-cap bullishness (MSFT/ORCL/PLTR), not directly evidenced. Capex skepticism vs. capex-beneficiary positioning: He doubts hyperscaler capex durability yet remains long MSFT and Oracle, which benefit from that same spend — his stock picks appear valuation-driven (ROE/earnings quality) rather than capex-narrative-driven, a distinction he doesn't reconcile. Exchanges (CME/CBOE/Nasdaq/ICE): Confidently contrarian ("cheap... not that big of a threat") but thin — no supporting valuation data or detail on the competitive threat given. Flag as a lead to verify, not a fleshed-out thesis. Meta: Genuinely split, deliberately unresolved — best-in-class AI monetization vs. explicit distrust of capital allocation ($80B metaverse loss). No stock call given. Investment Implications Microsoft (near-term, 2H 2026): Bull case (34% ROE/25% EPS growth vs. -23% YTD) is transcript-supported; but [inference] MSFT is also the largest capex spender among hyperscalers, so it sits at the intersection of his own bull thesis and his own bear mechanism (capex deceleration → multiple compression). The "rebalancing back into Microsoft" call may be more fragile than stated. Software as AI-trade hedge (multi-quarter, contingent on capex inflection): Stated plainly, not hedged. [Inference] If capex reversal is the real catalyst, software's outperformance is likely relative/rotational (least-ugly) rather than absolute — the infra-capex trade itself becoming the source of Mag-7-wide de-rating.
